title: SMTP DANE-TA: dNSName nameConstraints do not constrain a no-SAN leaf's CN
description:
## What

Composing RFC 5280 path validation with RFC 7672 CN fallback leaves a dNSName nameConstraint unable to constrain the name an intermediate vouches for, if the leaf omits its SAN.

pkix-chain/src/smtp.rs:332 runs, for TlsaUsage::DaneTa:

1. verify_chain(chain, [dane_anchor], ...) -- full RFC 5280 path validation, name constraints included.
2. verify_smtp_name(DaneTa, &chain[0], &identities) -> pkix_identity::verify_dns_name_with_cn_fallback.

Take a DANE-TA(2) anchor with a subordinate intermediate carrying dNSName nameConstraints (permitted: example.com, say), and a leaf with NO SAN extension and CN=victim.org:

* Step 1 passes. RFC 5280 section 4.2.1.10: 'Restrictions of the form dNSName, x400Address, ediPartyName, and registeredID MUST be applied only to the corresponding name type in subjectAltName.' No SAN means no dNSName to test, so the constraint has nothing to apply to.
* Step 2 matches. RFC 7672 section 3.2.3 keeps the CN-ID fallback 'only considered when no DNS-IDs are present', so CN=victim.org is matched against the reference identifier set.

Net: an intermediate constrained to example.com successfully vouches for victim.org. That is the exact outcome nameConstraints exist to prevent.

## Both halves are already proven in-tree

* Path half: the 748 bettertls::nameconstraints cases in pkix-difftest/baseline-limbo-analysis.md are precisely this shape -- no-SAN leaf, CN violating an intermediate's dNSName constraint, pkix-path passes. openssl fails them by applying its legacy CN-as-dNSName rule; pyca passes as we do. 660 of 748 have expected_result FAILURE.
* Identity half: pkix-identity/tests/verify_dns_name_cn_fallback.rs::cn_hostname_matches_when_there_is_no_san.

## Not a spec violation by either half

Both components follow their RFCs correctly, and neither RFC addresses the interaction. RFC 5280 does give CAs an answer: directoryName constraints 'MUST be applied to the subject field in the certificate (when the certificate includes a non-empty subject field)', so a CA wanting to constrain subject-DN naming must issue dirName constraints rather than dNSName ones. A CA that constrained only dNSName has, per the letter of the RFC, not constrained the subject DN.

So this is a composition hazard rather than a defect in either layer, which is why it was invisible: baseline-limbo-analysis.md justifies the path-layer behaviour by saying CN-as-dNSName 'should live in a separate pkix-tls / pkix-rfc6125 layer, not in pkix-path' -- and the layer that does consult the CN does not apply the path's constraints to it. Each half points at the other.

## Options

1. Document at both ends. The honest minimum: a caller composing these cannot currently see the hazard. Cheap, and it does not decide the question.
2. In the SMTP DANE path, refuse CN fallback when the validated path carried any dNSName nameConstraint. Needs the constraint state out of validate_path, which ValidatedPath does not currently expose.
3. Offer an opt-in WebPKI-strict mode in pkix-path applying dNSName constraints to the CN -- openssl's behaviour. Against the crate's stated scope, and would reclassify 748 corpus cases.

Recommend 1 now, 2 as the real fix if ValidatedPath can report it. Not proposing 3.

## Caveat on severity

Requires an attacker to control a name-constrained intermediate under an anchor the victim domain published in its own TLSA record. Narrow, but it is the threat model nameConstraints are for, and the mechanism is unconditional once reached.
